title: Vayigash: does my father live? (Genesis 45:3)
hookLine: Joseph's first words after "I am Joseph" are about his father
tomorrow: Vayigash: don't fall out on the way

cards: Judah has just finished speaking. He's described an old man at home who will die of grief if the youngest son doesn't come back. And the ruler of Egypt can't hold it in anymore.
He clears the room: everyone out. The servants go. Now it's only him and his brothers.
He cries so loudly the Egyptians hear it through the walls. Then he says two sentences. The first is the line people know.

teach.b: In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?" In Hebrew it's five words. Ani Yosef, I am Joseph.
Ha'od avi chai, is my father still alive? The brothers can't answer; they're terrified in front of him. Here's the puzzle the rabbis loved.
Joseph already knows the answer: Judah's whole speech was about their living father. So why ask? One answer: it isn't a question for information.
It's the first thing out of a son who hasn't seen his father since the day he was sold. The power, the grain, the revenge he could take all fall away, and what's left is: Dad. Is he really alive?
Some readers hear a rebuke underneath. You talk about our father's grief, Judah? Where was that concern the day you sold me?

A midrash says that when the brothers couldn't answer this one question, a sage later sighed: if a brother's words left them speechless, how will any of us answer on the day we're asked about our own lives?
Both readings can be true at once.
Then Joseph says, come near to me, please.
The same verb as yesterday. Judah drew near to plead; now Joseph asks all of them to draw near to be forgiven. The first thing a lost son asks about is the parent.
Joseph waited years to ask it out loud. Some people wait longer than they meant to.

how: Honoring father and mother is one of the Ten Commandments, and Jewish law spells it out in practical ways: providing for aging parents, standing when they enter, not contradicting them harshly, and saying Kaddish for them after they die.

o: and he rested, the portion of the seventh day
and he drew near, where Joseph says I am Joseph
and he built, the portion of the tower of Babel

games.q: the two sentences — tap the pairs.

s: Joseph asked because nobody had told him his father was alive
Judah had just spoken at length about their living father. that's why the rabbis ask why he asked.
Joseph sent everyone else out before revealing himself
he cleared the room, then wept so loudly the Egyptians heard.
some readers hear a rebuke in Joseph's question
where was your concern for our father when you sold me? the brothers had no answer.

games.q: you're Joseph. the room is empty except for the brothers who sold you. you've just said I am Joseph. what comes out next?
o: a list of what they did to you.
games.why: Joseph's next words were about his father: is he still alive? the brothers were too shaken to answer.

practice: Bring to mind one older person who shaped you: a parent, a grandparent, a teacher, an old neighbor, and picture their face. Ask Joseph's question in your own words: how are they, really?
If they're living, decide when you'll call; if they've died, let yourself remember one thing they used to say.

wordCard.voice: Vayigash. The portion where Joseph finally says I am Joseph, and his very next words ask after his father.

orig.note: Hebrew: is my father still alive? Joseph's words right after I am Joseph (Genesis 45:3).

carryVoice: Your line: doth my father yet live. Under all that power, he was still a son. Rest well.
